blocks.content: 1. Introduction

Picture your apartment building. The main door key opens the lobby. A different key opens your specific unit. Another one opens the mailbox. You would never tape a copy of your apartment key to the lobby noticeboard for convenience, even though it would save you a trip to the locksmith if you lose yours.
Yet that is basically what happens when a database password gets typed directly into a config file and pushed to GitHub. Anyone who can see that noticeboard now has a copy of your key, forever.

Secrets management is the discipline of keeping those keys, passwords, tokens, and certificates somewhere safe, handing them out only to the things that need them, and being able to change them without chaos. This topic covers what counts as a secret, why hardcoding them is such a persistent trap, and how real systems avoid it.
2. What counts as a secret
A secret is any piece of information that grants access to something, and would cause damage if the wrong person got hold of it. That definition is broader than most people first assume.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371094-661719403.png
blocks.alt: Database passwords, API keys, TLS private keys, and OAuth client secrets all feed into the category of secrets

blocks.content: 2.1 Common examples

["Database credentials, the username and password your app uses to connect to Postgres or MySQL.","API keys, for payment providers, email services, cloud SDKs, anything third party.","TLS private keys, the half of a certificate pair that must never leave your servers.","Encryption keys, used to encrypt and decrypt data at rest or in transit.","OAuth client secrets, used by your backend to prove its identity to an identity provider.","SSH keys and signing keys, used to access servers or sign releases."]
items: Database credentials, the username and password your app uses to connect to Postgres or MySQL.
API keys, for payment providers, email services, cloud SDKs, anything third party.
TLS private keys, the half of a certificate pair that must never leave your servers.
Encryption keys, used to encrypt and decrypt data at rest or in transit.
OAuth client secrets, used by your backend to prove its identity to an identity provider.
SSH keys and signing keys, used to access servers or sign releases.

blocks.title: The common thread
blocks.content: If leaking a piece of text would let a stranger read your database, impersonate your service, or decrypt your data, it is a secret. Treat it that way from day one, not after the first scare.
3. The classic mistake: hardcoding secrets

The easiest thing in the world is to type your database password straight into a config file, or paste an API key directly into a source file, so the app just works. It compiles, it connects, everyone moves on. This is also how almost every secret leak starts.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371094-750666993.png
blocks.alt: A secret typed into source code gets committed, pushed to a remote repo, and lives in git history forever

blocks.content: The moment that file is committed to version control, the secret is not just in your working directory anymore. It is in the commit history, and git history does not forget.
3.1 Why deleting it later does not help
blocks.text: 3.1 Why deleting it later does not help

blocks.content: Say someone notices the mistake a month later and removes the password from the file, then commits that change. The password is still sitting in the earlier commit. Anyone with clone access to the repo, or anyone who cloned it before the fix, still has it.

["Every developer who ever cloned the repo has a full copy of that old commit on their laptop.","CI systems, backup mirrors, and forks may hold copies you do not even know about.","Rewriting git history to scrub it is possible but painful, and does not undo copies that already exist elsewhere."]
items: Every developer who ever cloned the repo has a full copy of that old commit on their laptop.
CI systems, backup mirrors, and forks may hold copies you do not even know about.
Rewriting git history to scrub it is possible but painful, and does not undo copies that already exist elsewhere.

blocks.content: A secret committed to version control should be treated as permanently exposed. The only real fix is to rotate it, not to delete the line.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Making a repo private after the fact does not help either. If the secret was ever pushed while the repo was public, or ever seen by anyone outside your team, assume it is compromised and rotate it.
4. The core idea: a dedicated secrets manager
blocks.text: 4. The core idea: a dedicated secrets manager

blocks.content: The fix is to stop baking secrets into code or container images at all. Instead, secrets live in one dedicated, access controlled store, and applications fetch them at runtime or startup instead of carrying them around in their own files.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371095-447634352.png
blocks.alt: An application makes an authenticated call to a secrets manager, which returns the secret according to an access policy

blocks.content: 4.1 Access control is the whole point
blocks.text: 4.1 Access control is the whole point

blocks.content: A secrets manager is not just a fancy database for passwords. The value it adds is that every read is checked against a policy. Only the identities that are supposed to read a given secret can read it, and everything else is denied by default.

["A payments service can read the payments database credential, but not the marketing team analytics API key.","A human operator might be allowed to view a secret in an emergency, but that access itself gets logged.","Policies are defined once, centrally, instead of being reimplemented by every team that happens to store a secret somewhere."]
items: A payments service can read the payments database credential, but not the marketing team analytics API key.
A human operator might be allowed to view a secret in an emergency, but that access itself gets logged.
Policies are defined once, centrally, instead of being reimplemented by every team that happens to store a secret somewhere.

blocks.content: 5. How applications retrieve secrets
Moving secrets out of code only works if there is a clean way for the running application to get them back. There are a few common patterns, and most real systems combine more than one.
5.1 Authenticated fetch at startup

The application itself calls the secrets manager when it boots up. It first proves its own identity, usually with a short lived token or a certificate, and only then does the secrets manager hand over the actual secret value.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396371095-709185127.png
blocks.alt: An application authenticates to the secrets manager at startup, receives a short lived token, then fetches the secret

blocks.content: The secret typically only ever lives in memory after that, never written to disk, never baked into an image layer.
5.2 Injection by the orchestration platform

A lot of the time, the application does not talk to the secrets manager directly at all. Instead, the orchestration platform, think Kubernetes, pulls the secret and hands it to the container as an environment variable or a mounted file.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372732-34429051.png
blocks.alt: Kubernetes reads a Secret object and injects it into a pod either as an environment variable or a mounted volume file

blocks.content: ["Kubernetes Secrets can be exposed as environment variables, simple but they can leak into logs or crash dumps more easily.","Mounted files are generally preferred over env vars, since a file is less likely to get accidentally printed or logged.","The application code stays simple, it just reads an env var or a file path, unaware of where the value actually came from."]
items: Kubernetes Secrets can be exposed as environment variables, simple but they can leak into logs or crash dumps more easily.
Mounted files are generally preferred over env vars, since a file is less likely to get accidentally printed or logged.
The application code stays simple, it just reads an env var or a file path, unaware of where the value actually came from.

blocks.content: 5.3 The sidecar pattern
A middle ground is a sidecar container that runs next to your app, continuously syncing secrets from the vault and writing them to a shared, in memory volume the main app container can read from.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372734-427333810.png
blocks.alt: A sidecar container syncs secrets from Vault and writes them to a shared volume the app container reads

blocks.title: Why bother with a sidecar
blocks.content: It keeps the secrets manager client logic out of your application entirely. Your app just reads a local file, and the sidecar handles authentication, refresh, and renewal in the background.
6. Secret rotation
Rotation means changing a secret value periodically, or immediately after a suspected leak, without long downtime or a scramble across a dozen services.
6.1 Why you rotate

["Routine hygiene, an old credential that has been sitting unchanged for two years is just a bigger target than a fresh one.","Incident response, if you suspect a secret leaked, rotating it is the fastest way to shut the door.","Compliance, plenty of security standards simply require rotation on a schedule."]
items: Routine hygiene, an old credential that has been sitting unchanged for two years is just a bigger target than a fresh one.
Incident response, if you suspect a secret leaked, rotating it is the fastest way to shut the door.
Compliance, plenty of security standards simply require rotation on a schedule.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372734-744191346.png
blocks.alt: A secrets manager pushes a new secret value out to every service that consumes it

blocks.content: 6.2 Why it has to be designed in, not bolted on
blocks.text: 6.2 Why it has to be designed in, not bolted on

blocks.content: Here is the part that bites teams. If a secret is hardcoded in five different services, rotating it means finding all five, updating each config, redeploying each one, and hoping you did not miss a sixth place it was pasted. That is slow, error prone, and exactly why rotation gets skipped in practice.

With a secrets manager, rotation is a first class operation. The manager issues a new value, consuming services either pick it up automatically on their next fetch, or get a short grace period where both the old and new value work while things catch up.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: A secrets manager alone does not make rotation free. Your application still needs to handle a secret changing while it is running, whether that means reconnecting a database pool or reloading a client. Plan for that from the start instead of assuming a restart will always be available.
7. Protecting the store itself
A secrets manager is a single, high value target by design, since it holds the keys to everything else. Two things make that acceptable instead of terrifying.
7.1 Encryption at rest

Every secret sitting in the store is encrypted on disk, usually with a key managed by a separate key management service. Even someone with raw access to the underlying storage volume just sees ciphertext.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372735-598812137.png
blocks.alt: Secret values are encrypted before hitting storage, protected by a key from a separate KMS

blocks.content: 7.2 Audit logging
Every read gets logged: who or what asked for a secret, which secret, and exactly when. If something goes wrong later, you can answer the question that matters most: who touched this, and when.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372735-827010984.png
blocks.alt: A request for a secret gets checked against policy and a matching entry is written to an audit log

blocks.content: ["Detects unusual access patterns, like a service suddenly reading a secret it has never touched before.","Gives you a clean trail during an incident instead of guessing who had access.","Often required for compliance frameworks like SOC 2 or PCI DSS."]
items: Detects unusual access patterns, like a service suddenly reading a secret it has never touched before.
Gives you a clean trail during an incident instead of guessing who had access.
Often required for compliance frameworks like SOC 2 or PCI DSS.

blocks.content: 8. Real systems
You rarely build a secrets manager yourself. A handful of well tested options cover almost every real deployment.

{"headers":["System","What it is known for"],"rows":[["HashiCorp Vault","The most feature complete option, dynamic secrets, fine grained policies, works across any cloud or on prem setup."],["AWS Secrets Manager","Managed, integrates tightly with IAM, built in rotation for common database types."],["AWS Parameter Store","A simpler, cheaper sibling of Secrets Manager, fine for config values and secrets with lighter rotation needs."],["Kubernetes Secrets","Built directly into Kubernetes, convenient, but weaker on rotation, audit, and fine grained policy compared to a dedicated manager."],["Cloud provider KMS","Not a secrets manager on its own, but the encryption key layer that most of the above rely on underneath."]]}

blocks.title: A common real setup
blocks.content: Plenty of teams use Kubernetes Secrets for simple, low risk config, and layer in Vault or AWS Secrets Manager for anything that actually grants access to production data.
9. Trade-offs
None of this is free. A dedicated secrets manager is an extra moving part in your system, and it is worth being honest about the cost side.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Secrets never live in source code or images, closing off the most common leak path","One more external dependency your app now needs at startup to function"],["Rotation becomes a routine operation instead of a multi service scramble","Adds startup latency while the app authenticates and fetches secrets"],["Centralized access control and audit logging across every service","Requires running and securing yet another piece of infrastructure"],["Consistent policy enforcement instead of every team inventing its own approach","Overkill for a weekend project with one hobby API key and no real stakes"]]}

For a small side project, an environment variable read from a local .env file is usually fine. Past that, once real users, real money, or a real team are involved, the security and rotation benefits stop being optional.
10. Worked example: an order service fetching a DB credential
blocks.text: 10. Worked example: an order service fetching a DB credential

blocks.content: Say you run an order service that needs to connect to its Postgres database. The old way was a connection string sitting in a config file, password included, checked into the repo alongside everything else.

The new way: the order service authenticates to Vault when it boots, using an identity tied to its deployment, not a static password of its own. Vault hands back a short lived token. The service uses that token to request the actual database credential, which Vault can even generate on demand, unique to this one service instance.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372736-618438820.png
blocks.alt: The order service authenticates to Vault, receives a short lived database credential, then connects to the database

blocks.content: ["No database password ever appears in the order service repo or its deployment config.","The credential Vault issues can be scoped to expire in a few hours, so a leaked one is only useful briefly.","If the database credential needs to be rotated, Vault handles issuing new ones without anyone touching the order service code."]
items: No database password ever appears in the order service repo or its deployment config.
The credential Vault issues can be scoped to expire in a few hours, so a leaked one is only useful briefly.
If the database credential needs to be rotated, Vault handles issuing new ones without anyone touching the order service code.

Notice what is not in this file: no password, no connection string with credentials baked in, nothing checked into the repo that would grant database access on its own.

blocks.title: Gotcha: leases expire
blocks.content: Dynamic credentials like this come with a lease. If you forget to renew it before it expires, your database connections start failing at a random, inconvenient time. Build renewal into your service lifecycle from day one.

blocks.title: Gotcha: local development still needs a path
blocks.content: Not every laptop should authenticate against production Vault. Most teams give local development a separate, low privilege Vault namespace or a mocked secrets provider, so developers are not tempted to fall back to hardcoded values out of convenience.
12. The interview angle

Any system design question that involves a database, a third party API, or an internal service talking to another service, involves credentials somewhere. Interviewers notice whether you address that or quietly skip it.

["Never say a password or API key would just sit in a config file or environment variable with no further thought. That reads as a gap.","Mention a dedicated secrets manager, Vault or AWS Secrets Manager are both safe names to drop, plus how the application authenticates to it.","Bring up rotation explicitly. Saying how you would rotate a credential without redeploying every service is a very commonly expected detail.","If the design involves Kubernetes, knowing that Secrets exist but are weaker than a dedicated manager shows real depth."]
items: Never say a password or API key would just sit in a config file or environment variable with no further thought. That reads as a gap.
Mention a dedicated secrets manager, Vault or AWS Secrets Manager are both safe names to drop, plus how the application authenticates to it.
Bring up rotation explicitly. Saying how you would rotate a credential without redeploying every service is a very commonly expected detail.
If the design involves Kubernetes, knowing that Secrets exist but are weaker than a dedicated manager shows real depth.

blocks.content: You do not need to draw the entire Vault architecture on a whiteboard. You just need to show that credentials get a real answer instead of an afterthought.
13. Summary
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372737-487775468.png
blocks.alt: A hardcoded secret stays leaked forever, while a secrets manager keeps values rotated, audited, and encrypted

blocks.content: Secrets are anything that grants access and would hurt if it leaked: database passwords, API keys, TLS keys, encryption keys, OAuth secrets. Hardcoding any of them in source code or a committed config file means anyone with repo access has it forever, even after you delete the line.

The fix is a dedicated, access controlled secrets manager that applications call at startup, or that gets injected by the orchestration platform. Design for rotation, encryption at rest, and audit logging from the start, and a leaked or aging credential stops being a five alarm fire.
